title: WPMS/1551/2016 of Girish Chandra Dhasmana Vs Smt Madhavi Rawat

paras.text:
IN THE HIGH COURT OF UTTARAKHAND AT NAINITAL
Writ Petition no. 1551 of 2016 (M/S)
Girish Chandra Dhasmana ....... Petitioner
vs.
Smt. Madhavi Rawat ....... Respondent
Mr. D. Barthwal, Advocate for the petitioner.
Mr. Bhupesh Kandpal, Advocate for the respondent.
U. C. Dhyani, J. (Oral)
 By means of present writ petition, the petitioner
seeks to issue a writ, order or direction in the nature of
certiorari quashing the impugned order dated 02.06.2016,
passed by Civil Judge (Jr. Div.), Ramnagar in petitioner's
suit O.S. no. 24 of 2016, Girish Chandra Dhasmana vs Smt.
Mahavi Rawat (Annexure no. 1 to the petition), only to the
extent of non-grant of interim injunction in favour of the
petitioners herein, and may further be pleased to restrain
the defendant / respondent from carrying on or continuing
further works of construction over the petitioner's southern
damaged foundation without prior treatment of the leakage
and rectification of the damage to petitioner's southern
foundation, till the disposal of the petitioner's ad-interim
injunction application (paper no. 6C).
2) Counter affidavit filed on behalf of the
respondent today in the Court in taken on record.
3) The facts giving rise to the present writ petition
are that the petitioner has constructed a house over his free-hold plot, admeasuring 71.86 sq. mts., situated at Kotdwar

2
Road, Ramnagar and to the south of the said plot the house
of respondent exists. The free-hold was granted in favour
of the petitioner vide free-hold deed dated 13.01.2014, as
per Government Order of the State Government. Petitioner
constructed a double storey house, where he was currently
residing with his wife and old age mother. Prior to
petitioner's construction there exists the old house of
respondent on the southern side. The respondent started
constructing a new house by digging the foundations on
06.05.2016. Suddenly, on 08.05.2016, with the aid of JCB
machine, respondent started digging earth for erecting
columns at four corners of her land. Due to heavy and
careless digging of the earth by the JCB, the water
connections to the west of the respondent's plot towards the
petitioner's plot started leaking and water also started
pouring out of petitioner's southern foundation and filled
the pits dug by the respondent for her foundation and for
raising columns.
4) Due to negligent and violent JCB digging in
respect of foundation work of the respondent, the water
connections which were old, got damaged and it started
damaging petitioner's foundation and cracks started
developing on the floors, roof and walls of petitioner's
house. Petitioner made a representation to concerned
authorities. The employees of Jal Sansthan, Ramnagar
came to the site but could not identify the exact spot of
leakage and the said leakage is still continuing and exact
points of leakage could not be identified as yet.

3
5) On 01.06.2016, the respondent, however,
unfazed by the leakage started constructing beams and
columns of petitioner's southern end again damaging the
foundation of the respondent's house. On this, the
petitioner requested the respondent to stop the work, but the
respondent got violent and started challenging the
petitioner dare to stop her. It is alleged by the petitioner
that if the respondent carries on with her construction work
without remedying and rectifying the leakage, the same
will slowly corrode and destroy the petitioner's foundation
and other columns etc.
6) Thereafter, the petitioner immediately
approached the learned Civil Judge (Jr. Div.), Ramnagar by
filing suit in question for grant of perpetual injunction for
restraining the defendant / respondent, her agents, servants
and assigns from carrying on or continuing further work of
construction over the petitioner's southern damaged
foundation without prior treatment of the leakage and
rectification of the damage to the petitioner's southern
foundation. Alongwith the plaint, the petitioner also filed
application for ad-interim injunction (Paper no. 6C) for
restraining the respondent from carrying on construction till
the leakage of the water is remedied by the officials of the
Jal Sansthan. Petitioner also filed application under Rule
13, General Rules (Civil) for filing the said suit and for
entertaining the same during the ensuing Summer
Vacations in the Ramnagar Civil Courts.

4
7) Learned Civil Judge (Jr. Div.), Ramnagar vide
impugned order dated 02.06.2016, posted the interim
injunction application for 01.07.2016. Aggrieved against
the same, present writ petition has been filed on behalf of
the petitioner.
8) The submission of learned counsel for the
petitioner is that construction work being carried out by the
respondent in her plot is causing damage to the building of
the petitioner and because of digging the underground pipes
have been damaged and causing leakage in the foundation
of the petitioner's house.
9) It is the submission of learned counsel for the
respondent that the respondent is raising construction
strictly in accordance with the map sanctioned and
approved by the authority concerned. It is further
submitted that respondent alongwith other residents of the
locality moved the application before the Executive
Engineer, Uttarahand Jal Sansthan, Ramnagar, Nainital for
rectifying the leakage of the pipeline and the water is filed
up due to such leakage. It is pertinent to mention that the
said application dated 23.05.2016 was preferred before
filing of the suit, i.e., 02.06.2016. Respondent again, on
30.05.2016, moved the application complaining the
activities of the petitioner and further requested for the
inspection and the application of the respondent was
considered by the authorities and inspection was conducted
and finally verified and confirmed by the SDM, Ramnagar.
Thereafter, inspection was conducted and the report was

5
submitted before the SDM, Ramnagar, Nainital. In the
inspection it was revealed that the water is coming from the
house of the petitioner towards the respondent's house and
rather the respondent is suffering and then the petitioner
immediately preferred the present suit before trial court.
10) Without entering into the factual aspects of the
case, this Court would like to refer to the proposition of law
rendered in Rylands v. Fletcher, (1868) LR 3 HL 330,
which lays down the 'strict liability rule'. It was observed
by Lord Cranworth that "if a person brings, or accumulates,
on his land anything which, if it should escape, may cause
damage to his neighbour, he does so at his peril. If it does
escape, and cause damage, he is responsible, however
careful he may have been, and whatever precautions he
may have taken to prevent the damage." It was observed
by Lord Cairns LC that "the defendants, treating them as
the owners or occupiers of the close on which the reservoir
was constructed, might lawfully have used that close for
any purpose for which it might in the ordinary course of the
enjoyment of land be used; and if, in what I may term the
natural user of that land, there had been any accumulation
of water, either on the surface or underground, and if, by
the operation of the laws of nature, that accumulation of
water had passed off into the close occupied by the
Plaintiff, the Plaintiff could not have complained that that
result had taken place. If he had desired to guard himself
against it, it would have lain upon him to have done so, by
leaving, or by interposing, some barrier between his close
and the close of the Defendants in order to have prevented

6
that operation of the laws of nature...On the other hand if
the Defendants, not stopping at the natural use of their
close, had desired to use it for any purpose which I may
term a non-natural use, for the purpose of introducing into
the close that which in its natural condition was not in or
upon it, for the purpose of introducing water either above
or below ground in quantities and in a manner not the result
of any work or operation on or under the land, - and if in
consequence of their doing so, or in consequence of any
imperfection in the mode of their doing so, the water came
to escape and to pass off into the close of the Plaintiff, then
it appears to me that that which the Defendants were doing,
they were doing at their own peril; and, if in the course of
their doing it, the evil arose to which I have referred, the
evil, namely, of the escape of the water and its passing
away to the close of the Plaintiff and injuring the Plaintiff,
then for the consequence of that, in my opinion, the
Defendants would be liable."
11) The principle of Rylands v. Fletcher (supra)
has been followed in several Indian cases, a summary of
which is being given here-in-below for convenience:
 "A suit for damages was held to lie against a
proprietor who penned back the water of a stream by
erecting a bund upon his land, so as to inundate the land
of his neighbour, without his license and consent:
Becharam Chowdhary v. Puhubnath Jha, (1869) 2 Beng
LR (Appex.) 53. The defendant closed up the outlet of a
bank upon his own land, whereby the surface drainage
water had immemorially flowed from the plaintiff's land
into and over the defendant's land and so escaped. By

7
reason of the closing of those outlets the water was
unable to escape, and the plaintiff's land became flooded
and the crops therein damaged. It was held that the
defendant was liable for the damage caused: Mussamut
Annundmoyee Dossee vs Mussamut Hameedoonissa,
(1862) Marsh. 85, sub-nom. Must. Hameedoonissa vs
Musst. Anundmoyee Dossee, (1862) 1 Hay 152.
 The Bombay High Court has held that before a person
can be made liable in damages for injury cause to his
neighbour's land by water either flowing from the
former's land to the latter's or percolating from the one
into the other it must be shown that the water was
brought or collected on his land by him voluntarily for
his own purposes in a non-natural use of it. Otherwise he
is not liable: Moholal vs Bai Jivkore, (1904) 6 Bom LR
529: ILR 28 Bom 472. This case has been doubted and
distinguished in Ramanuja Chariar vs Krishnaswami
Mudali, (1907) ILR 31 Mad 169, which decided that the
retention of water by a person on a portion of his land to
prevent its passing on to other portions of his land was
not an act done in the natural and usual course of
enjoyment and the person so doing was liable for damage
caused thereby.
 A suit for damages, based on an allegation that
defendant had neglected to drain his garden so as to
prevent water from collecting there and injuring the
adjoining property of the plaintiff is not maintainable as
the owner of property is under no legal obligation to
incur expenses upon it for the benefit of his neighbours,
where it has not been altered in character by his acts or
with his permission in such a way as to expose them to
any injury : Baldeo Das v. Secretary of State, (1883) PR
no. 30 of 1883.

8
 Where the defendants with a view to make their land
cultivable lowered its level with the consequence that
water in a tank belonging to a third party passed to that
land and subsequently overflowed into lands belonging to
the plaintiff, it was held that the plaintiff was not entitled
to any cause of action: Kenaram Akhuli v. Sristidhar
Chatterjee, (1912)16 CWN 875.
 Where Government constructs an irrigation canal it
undertakes a duty to protect other parties against damage
arising from the water of the canal and if it does not take
adequate precautions to deal with the overflow of water
from the canal, for instance, by means of an outlet at the
tail end of the canal, it is liable to compensate those to
whom damage may be caused by such overflow:
Secretary of State for India in Council v. Ramtahal Ram,
(1925) 6 PLT 708.
 The retention of water by a person on a portion of his
land to prevent its passing on to the other portions of his
land is not an act done in the natural and usual course of
enjoyment and the person so doing is liable for damage
caused thereby : Dhanusao v. Sitabai, ILR 1948 Nag 698.
 Where the defendant set fire to his land without taking
necessary precaution to prevent the same from spreading
into the lands in the neighbourhood, he was 'playing with
fire' and to be deemed to have foreseen the possibility of
the fire spreading into the lands adjoining his land and is
liable for any damage caused to them: M. Madapa v. K.
Kariappa, AIR 1964 Mys 80.
 Where the defendant installed a big ore melting
furnace near the plaintiff's house, he was held liable for
emission of harmful gases with offensive smell and
heating causing discomfort : Darshan Ram v. Nazar
Ram, AIR 1989 P&H 253."

9
12) It was further held in Dhanusao v. Sitabai, ILR
(1948) Nag 698 that the rule of Rylands v. Fletcher applies
only if the defendant brings or accumulates on his own land
something that is likely to escape and do mischief,
irrespective of the question whether that was done by the
defendant willfully or negligently.
13) In Musgrove v. Pandelis, (1919) 2 KB 43 it was
held that if a man brings on to his premises a dangerous
thing which is liable to cause fire, such as a motor-car with
petrol in it, the carburetor of which is not unlikely to get on
fire when the engine is started, and a fire results and
escapes causing damage to adjoining property, though
without any negligence on his part, he is liable, for the rule
is that he must keep such a thing under control at his peril.
In Hale v. Jenning Bros., (1938) 1 All ER 579, it was held
that a person who brings dangerous substance upon
premises and carries on a dangerous trade with them is
liable if, though without negligence on his part, these
substances cause injury to persons or property in their
neighbourhood."
[Excerpts from 'The Law of Torts' by
Ratanlal & Dhirajlal, 24th Edition, 2002]
14) In the instant case, this fact is not under dispute
that the defendant / respondent is constructing house in her
own land. It is also not in dispute that the plaintiff and
defendant (petitioner and respondent herein) are the
neighbours. A duty is, therefore, cast upon the defendant
(respondent herein) to construct her house in such a way

10
that it does not cause damage to his neighbour, i.e., the
petitioner.
15) Learned counsel for the respondent stated that
no damage has been caused to the house of the petitioner
and, on receiving instructions from his client, further stated
that no damage will be caused to petitioner's house in
future as well.
16) Recording the submission of learned counsel
for the parties, the writ petition is disposed of in the light of
principle of law laid down by House of Lords in Rylands v.
Fletcher (supra).
17) It is, however, made clear that this order is only
for the interregnum, inasmuch as the suit is already pending
adjudication before the court below and 01.07.2016 is fixed
for hearing on ad-interim injunction application and
objections thereon.
18) The trial court shall pass an order on paper no.
6C and objections thereon, in accordance with law, and
untrammeled by any of the observations made by this Court
in the body of the judgment.
 [Stay application no. 5514 of 2016 also stands
disposed of.]
